# Mahārāhulovāda Sutta (MN 62 (PTS MN i 420))

**ID:** MN 62 (PTS MN i 420)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahārāhulovāda Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 420
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahārāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 62; PTS MN i 420–426) is the sixty-second discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, set at Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthi [Lamotte 1988; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The sutta begins while the Buddha and his son Rāhula are going for alms; the Buddha instructs Rāhula to contemplate all material form—past, present, or future, internal or external—as not-self ("not mine, not I, not my self") [Radich 2007]. After Sāriputta separately advises Rāhula to practice mindfulness of breathing, Rāhula approaches the Buddha for instruction. The Buddha presents a broad meditative curriculum prior to breath contemplation: Rāhula is taught to contemplate the internal and external physical elements (earth, water, fire, wind, and space), using them as metaphors to cultivate endurance and impartiality without aversion or attachment [Polak 2011; Anālayo 2016; Tzungkuen Wen]. This is followed by the cultivation of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the perception of unattractiveness (*asubha*), and the perception of impermanence (*anicca*) [Anālayo 2016]. Finally, the Buddha details the complete sixteen-step scheme of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), declaring that its mastery ensures mindful awareness even of one's final breaths [Anālayo 2016; Anālayo 2019].

Curated parallels include *Ekottarika-āgama* discourse EĀ 17.1, chapter 20 of the *Arthaviniścaya*, *Saṁyutta Nikāya* 54.1, *Saṁyuktāgama* parallels (SĀ 803, SĀ 815, SĀ³ 15), Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 84), and Vinaya *Pārājika* 3 [Lamotte 1988; Anālayo 2019]. As noted by Anālayo, EĀ 17.1 preserves only the initial three steps of the sixteen-step breathing formula due to text corruption and reworking [Anālayo 2019]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse: the element analysis corresponds closely with the *Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta* (MN 140, §8.1–12.9) and *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta* (MN 28, §10.1–10.9), while the breath-meditation sections align verbatim with SN 54 and MN 118 [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns the text's element and mindfulness formulas with passages in Candrakīrti's *Prasannapadā*, the *Satyasiddhiśāstra*, the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, and the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* [DharmaNexus].
